texts.exact_text: Ta Kwang indicates that (under the conditions which it symbolises) it will be advantageous to be firm and correct.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 34; scan-backed transcription p. 129, hexagram statement
texts.notes: Legge's title restored from the source statement.

texts.exact_text: The first NINE, undivided, shows its subject manifesting his strength in his toes. But advance will lead to evil, -- most certainly.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 34; scan-backed transcription p. 129, line 1

texts.exact_text: The second NINE, undivided, shows that with firm correctness there will be good fortune.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 34; scan-backed transcription p. 129, line 2

texts.exact_text: The third NINE, undivided, shows, in the case of a small man, one using all his strength; and in the case of a superior man, one whose rule is not to do so. Even with firm correctness the position would be perilous. (The exercise of strength in it might be compared to the case of) a ram butting against a fence, and getting his horns entangled.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 34; scan-backed transcription p. 129, line 3

texts.exact_text: The fourth NINE, undivided, shows (a case in which) firm correctness leads to good fortune, and occasion for repentance disappears. (We see) the fence opened without the horns being entangled. The strength is like that in the wheel-spokes of a large waggon.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 34; scan-backed transcription p. 129, line 4

texts.exact_text: The fifth SIX, divided, shows one who loses his ram(-like strength) in the ease of his position. (But) there will be no occasion for repentance.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 34; scan-backed transcription p. 129, line 5

texts.exact_text: The sixth SIX, divided, shows (one who may be compared to) the ram butting against the fence, and unable either to retreat, or to advance as he would fain do. There will not be advantage in any respect; but if he realise the difficulty (of his position), there will be good fortune.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 34; scan-backed transcription p. 129, line 6

texts.exact_text:
The strong lines predominate in Ta Kwang. It suggested to king Wén a state or condition of things in which there was abundance of strength and vigour. Was strength alone enough for the conduct of affairs? No. He saw also in the figure that which suggested to him that strength should be held in subordination to the idea of right, and exerted only in harmony with it.

This is the lesson of the hexagram ䷡, as sententiously expressed in the Tuàn.

Line 1 is strong, in its correct place, and also the first line in Khien, the hexagram of strength, and the first line in Ta Kwang. The idea of the figure might seem to be concentrated in it; and hence we have it symbolised by strength in the toes, or advancing. But such a measure is too bold to be undertaken by one in the lowest place, and moreover there is no proper correlate in 4. Hence comes the evil auspice.

Line 2 is strong, but the strength is tempered by its being in an even place, instead of being excited by it, as might be feared. Then the place is that in the centre. With firm correctness there will be good fortune.

Line 3 is strong, and in its proper place. It is at the top moreover of ☰ Qián. A small man so symbolled will use his strength to the utmost; but not so the superior man. For him the position is beyond the safe middle, and he will be cautious; and not injure himself, like the ram, by exerting his strength.

Line 4 is still strong, but in the place of a weak line; and this gives occasion to the cautions with which the symbolism commences. The subject of the line going forward thus cautiously, his strength will produce good effects, such as are described.

Line 5 is weak, and occupies a central place. Its subject will cease therefore to exert his strength; but this hexagram does not forbid the employment of strength, but would only control and direct it. All that is said about him is that he will give no occasion for repentance.

Line 6 being at the top of ☳ Zhèn, the symbol of movement, and at the top of Ta Kwang, its subject may be expected to be active in exerting his strength; and through his weakness, the result would be as described. But he becomes conscious of his weakness, reflects and rests, and good fortune results, as he desists from the prosecution of his unwise efforts. 大壮 ䷡
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 34; scan-backed transcription p. 129, notes

texts.exact_text: 大壯：利貞。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/大壯; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 34, 易經卦辭

texts.exact_text: 大壯，大者壯也。剛以動，故壯。大壯利貞；大者正也。正大而天地之情可見矣！
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/大壯; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 34, 彖

texts.exact_text: 雷在天上，大壯；君子以非禮弗履。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/大壯; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 34, 大象

texts.exact_text: 初九：壯于趾，征凶，有孚。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/大壯; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 34, 爻 1

texts.exact_text: 壯于趾，其孚窮也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/大壯; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 34, 小象 1

texts.exact_text: 九二：貞吉。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/大壯; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 34, 爻 2

texts.exact_text: 九二貞吉，以中也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/大壯; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 34, 小象 2

texts.exact_text: 九三：小人用壯，君子用罔，貞厲。羝羊觸藩，羸其角。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/大壯; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 34, 爻 3

texts.exact_text: 小人用壯，君子罔也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/大壯; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 34, 小象 3

texts.exact_text: 九四：貞吉悔亡，藩決不羸，壯于大輿之輹。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/大壯; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 34, 爻 4

texts.exact_text: 藩決不羸，尚往也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/大壯; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 34, 小象 4

texts.exact_text: 六五：喪羊于易，无悔。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/大壯; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 34, 爻 5

texts.exact_text: 喪羊于易，位不當也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/大壯; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 34, 小象 5

texts.exact_text: 上六：羝羊觸藩，不能退，不能遂，无攸利，艱則吉。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/大壯; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 34, 爻 6

texts.exact_text: 不能退，不能遂，不詳也。艱則吉，咎不長也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/大壯; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 34, 小象 6

texts.exact_text:
In Ta Kwang we see that which is great becoming strong. We have the (trigram ☳) denoting strength directing that which denotes movement, and hence (the whole) is expressive of vigour.

'Ta Kwang indicates that it will be advantageous to be firm and correct:' -- that which is great (should be) correct. Given correctness and greatness (in their highest degree), and the character and tendencies of heaven and earth can be seen.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix I, Hexagram 34, p. 241

texts.exact_text: (The trigram ☰ representing) heaven and above it ☳ that for thunder form Ta Kwang. The superior man, in accordance with this, does not take a step which is not according to propriety.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 34, p. 310

texts.exact_text: 'He manifests his vigour in his toes:' -- this will certainly lead to exhaustion.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 34, line 1, p. 310

texts.exact_text: 'The second NINE, (undivided), shows that with firm correctness there will be good fortune:' -- this is due to its being in the centre, (and its subject exemplifying the due mean).
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 34, line 2, p. 310

texts.exact_text: 'The small man uses all his strength; in the case of the superior man it is his rule not to do so.'
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 34, line 3, p. 310

texts.exact_text: 'The fence is opened and the horns are not entangled:' -- (the subject of the line) still advances.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 34, line 4, p. 310

texts.exact_text: 'He loses his ram and hardly perceives it:' -- he is not in his appropriate place.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 34, line 5, p. 310

texts.exact_text: 'He is unable either to retreat or to advance:' -- this is owing to his want of care. 'If he realise the difficulty (of his position), there will be good fortune:' -- his error will not be prolonged.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 34, line 6, p. 310
